summary: Provincial R&D tax credits in Canada supplement the federal SR&ED program, with every province except Prince Edward Island, along with the Yukon, offering its own incentive. Quebec's CRIC offers refundable 30% and 20% rates, Ontario combines the OITC, ORDTC and OBRITC, B.C. provides a permanent 10% credit and Alberta's IEG pays 8% to 20%. Provincial credits reduce federal qualified expenditures under the grind rule.

Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Tax Law

Canada maintains one of the most mature and financially significant research and development fiscal regimes in the industrialized world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program. The legislative lineage of the Canadian R&D tax framework traces back to 1944 amendments to the Income War Tax Act—the statutory predecessor to the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA)—which first permitted Canadian corporations to deduct research and development outlays against business revenue, creating an explicit statutory exception to the general capital expenditure prohibition set out in section 18 of the ITA. The modern volume-based investment tax credit architecture was established in 1983 and is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance across the country through six coordinating tax offices. In the fiscal year ending March 2026, the federal SR&ED program delivered $4.6 billion in investment tax credits across more than 24,000 corporate and unincorporated claims.

Between late 2024 and spring 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative and administrative transformation in more than a decade. Following a two-phase public consultation conducted by the Department of Finance between January 31, 2024, and May 27, 2024, alongside legislative proposals in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the 2025 Federal Budget (Canada Strong), Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Projected to inject $2.1 billion in net new federal support over the five-year fiscal horizon from 2025–2026 to 2029–2030, the Bill C-15 reforms fundamentally recalibrate corporate innovation economics for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Concurrently, provincial regimes executed structural overhauls—most notably Quebec's replacement of its legacy R&D tax architecture with the consolidated Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, or CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and British Columbia's enactment of Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) making the B.C. SR&ED credit permanent and harmonizing its thresholds with federal law.
Dual-Mechanism Federal Structure: Section 37 Pooling and Section 127 Credits

The federal SR&ED regime operates through a bifurcated statutory mechanism under the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). The first pillar is the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool governed by subsection 37(1) of the ITA. Under this provision, qualifying SR&ED expenditures of a current nature—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible capital expenditures—incurred in Canada are accumulated in a dedicated tax pool. A taxpayer may deduct any portion of this pool to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year or elect to carry undeducted pooled balances forward indefinitely to shelter taxable income in future taxation years. This elective deferral mechanism is particularly advantageous for corporate claimants seeking to utilize expiring non-capital losses, foreign tax credits, or non-refundable investment tax credits prior to drawing down their SR&ED deduction pool.

The second pillar is the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit (ITC), governed primarily by subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the ITA. In addition to claiming the subsection 37(1) income deduction, a claimant earns an SR&ED ITC calculated as a statutory percentage—ranging from the 15% basic rate to the 35% enhanced rate—of its "qualified expenditures" as defined under subsection 127(9). Depending on the claimant's corporate classification, expenditure volume, and asset nature, the ITC may be applied to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, refunded directly in cash, or carried back three taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset federal tax payable in those periods.

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Originally housed in Regulation 2900(1) and subsequently elevated into subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" is legally defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition encompasses three primary research categories and one restricted category of commensurate support work. Under paragraph (a), basic research comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (c), experimental development is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Across Canadian corporate filings, experimental development accounts for the vast majority of industrial, software, and manufacturing claims.

Complementing those three core categories, paragraph (d) of the definition in subsection 248(1) admits work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, the statutory definition expressly excludes commercial activities and non-technological disciplines from SR&ED qualification, barring claims for market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
The 2025–2026 Federal Legislative Overhaul (Bill C-15)

The enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) on March 26, 2026, resolved longstanding structural bottlenecks in Canada's innovation tax policy. Prior to these reforms, macroeconomic analyses of the Canadian innovation ecosystem identified a pronounced "scale-up penalty": Canadian firms aggressively utilized the 35% refundable SR&ED rate at the seed stage, but rapidly lost access to enhanced refundable support once they raised institutional venture capital—which inflated their balance-sheet taxable capital above $10 million—or completed an initial public offering on a Canadian exchange. Furthermore, the 2012 federal budget's elimination of capital expenditure eligibility, which took effect after 2013, heavily penalized hardware-intensive industries such as clean technology, advanced manufacturing, robotics, semiconductors, and life sciences relative to pure-play software companies whose cost structures are dominated by labour. Bill C-15 addresses these structural distortions through four foundational legislative amendments applicable to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), alongside capital property rules taking effect for acquisitions made after December 15, 2024.
Doubling the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit to $6 Million

While the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 doubled the baseline expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million per taxation year. For a qualifying corporation incurring $6 million in current SR&ED expenditures, the maximum annual refundable federal ITC doubles from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000, delivering an immediate $1.05 million annual cash-flow injection. Associated corporations must allocate this $6 million annual expenditure limit among members of the associated corporate group using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit).
Extension of the Enhanced 35% Rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, only Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) qualified for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC, while public corporations and companies controlled by public corporations were restricted to the basic 15% non-refundable rate regardless of their operational scale. Under the Bill C-15 amendments, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) can now claim the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada (or have elected to be a public corporation), not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons, and satisfy the statutory gross revenue phase-out thresholds. This reform removes the tax disincentive that previously penalized high-growth Canadian technology, clean-tech, and life-sciences firms for listing on Canadian public markets.
Expanded Phase-Out Thresholds ($15M–$75M) and Elective Gross Revenue Formula

To prevent scaling businesses from prematurely phasing out of the enhanced 35% rate, Bill C-15 increased the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range by 50%, moving the lower threshold from $10 million to $15 million and the upper elimination threshold from $50 million to $75 million across the associated corporate group (the former prior-year taxable income test had already been repealed for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019). In addition, Bill C-15 introduced an elective revenue-based phase-out mechanism for CCPCs—and mandated this revenue-based phase-out structure for ECPCs—under which the $6 million expenditure limit is phased out over the exact same $15 million to $75 million corridor based on the corporation's average gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years. This structural flexibility ensures that venture-backed biotechnology, clean energy, or hardware CCPCs holding $40 million to $70 million in equity or debt capital on their balance sheets while generating minimal pre-commercial revenue can elect the gross revenue test and retain their full $6 million expenditure limit.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

Reversing the 11-year exclusion that applied from January 1, 2014, to December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures for property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 37(1.2) of the ITA, new depreciable property—such as R&D laboratory and testing equipment, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, and experimental infrastructure, but strictly excluding buildings or leasehold interests in buildings—acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifies for both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool (as deemed capital cost allowance) and subsection 127(9) ITCs if the claimant intends, at the time of acquisition, either to use the property during all or substantially all (≥ 90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in SR&ED carried out in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (≥ 90%) of the property's value in the prosecution of SR&ED carried out in Canada. Used equipment remains strictly ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives.

Alongside all-or-substantially-all capital assets, Bill C-15 reinstated the regime for Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under the definitions of "qualified expenditure," "first term shared-use-equipment," and "second term shared-use-equipment" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. New depreciable property (other than prescribed depreciable property that was intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is used primarily (> 50% but < 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during its first period (a minimum of 12 months ending at the first taxation year-end at least 12 months after acquisition) and second period (ending at the first taxation year-end at least 24 months after acquisition) qualifies for 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost per term as a qualified expenditure. Across both the first and second terms, up to 50% of the capital cost of SUE earns SR&ED ITCs, calculated without reference to borrowed money costs and after non-arm's length adjustments under subsection 127(11.6). Any ITC earned on SUE and applied to reduce taxes payable or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of the relevant capital cost allowance class in the subsequent taxation year.

Furthermore, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, were restored to eligibility, overturning the former paragraph 37(8)(d) exclusion that barred leasing capital property between 2014 and December 15, 2024. Where leased equipment is used all or substantially all (≥ 90%) in SR&ED, 100% of the lease payment qualifies; where leased equipment is used primarily (50% to under 90%) for SR&ED, claimants electing the Traditional Method claim the attributable portion as overhead on Line 360 of Form T661, whereas claimants electing the Proxy Method claim 50% of the lease cost on Line 355 (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture). Finally, the restoration of capital eligibility eliminated the former subsections 37(14) and 37(15) "capital look-through rule"—which prior to December 16, 2024, required a claimant to reduce SR&ED contract and third-party payments by any capital/depreciable property expenditures of the performer and mandated written notification within 90 days of calendar year-end—while simultaneously reintroducing subsection 127(11.6) non-arm's length capital cost restrictions effective December 16, 2024.
Matrix of Federal ITC Rates and Refundability Rules (2025–2026)

A critical technical distinction reinforced by the CRA and OECD statutory analyses under Bill C-15 is the differential refundability between expenditures of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount) and capital expenditures. While current expenditures within the $6 million expenditure limit earn a 100% refundable 35% credit for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs, credits earned at the 35% enhanced rate on restored capital expenditures (and shared-use equipment) are 40% refundable, yielding an immediate cash refund equal to 14% of the capital cost plus 21% in non-refundable ITCs available to offset federal tax payable.

body.text: To illustrate the compounding cash-flow mechanics of these tiers, consider a qualifying CCPC with prior-year taxable capital below $15 million that incurs $8,000,000 in current qualified SR&ED expenditures during its 2026 taxation year. On the first $6,000,000 of expenditures falling within the annual expenditure limit, the corporation earns the enhanced 35% ITC of $6,000,000 × 35% = $2,100,000, which is 100% refundable in cash. On the remaining $2,000,000 of current expenditures exceeding the $6 million expenditure limit, because the corporation is an un-phased-out qualifying CCPC, it earns the basic 15% ITC of $2,000,000 × 15% = $300,000, of which 40% is refundable in cash, generating an additional $300,000 × 40% = $120,000 in immediate cash refund (with the remaining $180,000 of non-refundable ITCs available to offset Part I tax payable or carry back 3 and forward 20 years). Consequently, the corporation's total immediate cash refund for the year reaches $2,100,000 + $120,000 = $2,220,000.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Specified Employee Restrictions
Granular Rules for Qualifying Expenditure Categories

To enter the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base, outlays must satisfy strict statutory timing, territorial, and nexus requirements administered under CRA policies.
Salaries and Wages (T4 Remuneration)

Eligible salaries and wages encompass gross employment remuneration reported on a T4 slip incurred for employees performing SR&ED in Canada, alongside a restricted statutory allowance for permissible SR&ED wages of Canadian-resident employees performing integral support work outside Canada capped at 10% of total in-Canada directly engaged SR&ED salaries. Under the unpaid remuneration rule in subsection 78(4) of the ITA, accrued salaries, wages, or bonuses must be paid in the taxation year or within 180 days after the end of the taxation year to be deductible and eligible in that year. Unpaid remuneration that remains outstanding more than 180 days after fiscal year-end is denied in the year incurred and can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (entered on Line 310 of Form T661), though such late-paid prior-year wages are permanently excluded from the Prescribed Proxy Amount salary base. Taxable benefits may be included in SR&ED wages only if they represent a cash outlay or a reasonable estimate of actual employer costs excluding GST/HST or PST, provided those underlying costs are not also deducted elsewhere as a business expense.

Per the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, several categories of employment-related outlays are strictly excluded from direct SR&ED salaries and wages. First, the employer's share of related payroll benefits—including statutory contributions to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), provincial Employer Health Tax (EHT), Workers' Compensation boards, and group medical or pension plans—is excluded from direct SR&ED wages; these related benefits can only be claimed as overhead under the Traditional Method, as they are deemed captured by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method. Second, remuneration paid for periods of extended vacation or sick leave is excluded because the employee is neither directly engaged in nor directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED during those absences. Third, employee stock option benefits do not constitute an expenditure for SR&ED and are completely ineligible. Fourth, retiring allowances cannot be claimed as SR&ED salaries or under the Proxy Method, though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method. Fifth, dividends paid to shareholder-researchers or founders are distributions of after-tax corporate earnings rather than salary or wages; paying owner-managers in dividends rather than T4 payroll completely forfeits both direct SR&ED wage credits and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.
Materials Consumed or Transformed

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA (applicable to the Proxy Method) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR (applicable to the Traditional Method), a claimant may include the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed are items rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimental trials, whereas materials transformed are physical inputs integrated into an experimental prototype, custom product, pilot plant, or experimental production run. All claimed materials must be paid for in the taxation year or within 180 days of fiscal year-end. General laboratory supplies or shop items that are neither physically incorporated into the experimental object nor destroyed during testing are classified as overhead rather than materials, rendering them claimable only under the Traditional Method.
Cloud Computing, Hosting Infrastructure, and Third-Party APIs

In modern software, SaaS, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing SR&ED claims, cloud computing expenditures—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure—alongside third-party development APIs represent a substantial expenditure component. Under CRA administrative guidelines and the Bill C-15 software and infrastructure enhancements, cloud computing and software fees directly utilized to train machine learning models, run experimental simulations, or host non-production R&D development and staging environments are eligible for SR&ED incentives. However, CRA financial reviewers enforce a strict accounting separation between production cloud infrastructure—which constitutes Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) or Cost of Revenue used to deliver live commercial SaaS applications to paying customers—and development or staging R&D infrastructure. Claimants must implement environment resource tagging in their cloud consoles, exporting monthly AWS, GCP, or Azure billing reports coded by production versus development/staging SR&ED project tags to substantiate the exact portion of cloud compute consumed in systematic experimentation. Where a startup utilizes promotional cloud credits such as AWS Activate, only net out-of-pocket expenditures actually incurred by the claimant qualify for SR&ED credits.
Subcontractors (Arm's-Length and Non-Arm's Length) and Third-Party Payments

Payments made to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors performing SR&ED work directly on behalf of the claimant in Canada are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, but since January 1, 2013, only 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies as a "qualified expenditure" for computing the Section 127 ITC. Similarly, third-party payments made to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D consortia for SR&ED related to the claimant's business (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results) are 100% deductible under Section 37 and 80% eligible for Section 127 ITCs, and must be reported on Form T1263. Conversely, expenditures paid to a non-arm's length (NAL) subcontractor do not earn ITCs in the hands of the payer directly; instead, the NAL performer incurs the underlying SR&ED expenditures and the parties may jointly elect to transfer the qualified expenditures to the NAL payer by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length).
The Overhead Election: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

Pursuant to subsection 37(10) of the ITA, a taxpayer must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method on Line 160 or the Traditional Method on Line 162. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method is locked in and irrevocable for that year.

Under the Proxy Method—governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR—the claimant does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661, entering $0 on Line 360. Instead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 (entered on Line 502) equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. A fundamental statutory asymmetry governs the PPA: because the PPA is a notional calculation rather than an actual cash outlay, it cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, nor can the underlying overhead expenses that the PPA represents be added to the section 37 pool (instead, those actual overhead expenses are deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA). Crucially, however, the PPA is included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9), earning the full 35% (or 15%) SR&ED ITC. Under subsection 2900(6) of the ITR, the PPA is subject to an overall cap ensuring it cannot exceed the corporation's total business deductions for the year less specified deductions such as capital cost allowance, section 37 deductions, interest, and building costs.

Under the Traditional Method—governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR—the claimant enters $0 on Lines 355 and 502 and itemizes actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360. To qualify under the Traditional Method, every claimed overhead expenditure must be proven to be directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED in Canada) and incremental, meaning the cost would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out. While record-keeping under the Traditional Method is complex, large industrial or shop-floor claimants whose actual incremental overhead exceeds 55% of direct wages can utilize it to claim support and administrative salaries, employer payroll benefits, employee training and relocation costs, retiring allowances, shop-floor utilities, and property taxes in both the section 37 pool and the section 127 ITC base.

body.text: Specified Employee Restrictions (Owner-Managers and 10% or Greater Shareholders)

Because owner-managers of private corporations exercise direct control over their own remuneration, the ITA and ITR impose two distinct statutory ceilings on specified employees—defined in subsection 248(1) as any employee who is a "specified shareholder" (owning directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, including shares owned by non-arm's length persons) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer, such as a spouse, sibling, child, or parent of a controlling shareholder.

The first ceiling restricts the direct SR&ED wage pool under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA. Under this provision, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are 100% disallowed for SR&ED purposes. Furthermore, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year. For the 2026 calendar year, the YMPE is $74,600, establishing a maximum direct SR&ED salary cap of 5 × $74,600 = $373,000. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including certain related individuals and partnerships deemed to be associated corporations), this 5 × YMPE ceiling must be allocated among them by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development), accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement (or a sole-shareholder signed confirmation), on or before the corporations' respective SR&ED reporting deadlines; failure to timely file Form T1174 deems the specified employee's SR&ED salary to be nil.

The second ceiling restricts the Proxy Method salary base under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the ITR. Under ITR subsection 2900(9), for every employee—whether specified or arm's-length—bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year are excluded from the PPA salary base. Under ITR subsection 2900(7), the maximum amount that a claimant can include in the PPA salary base for each specified employee is further restricted to the lesser of the employee's directly engaged SR&ED salary, 75% of the specified employee's total base salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages), or 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the year (with no proration for the portion of the year the individual was not a specified employee):
PPA Base<sub>Spec</sub> = min(SR&ED Salary, 0.75 × Total Base Salary, 2.5 × YMPE × Days Employed ÷ 365)

For a full 365-day taxation year ending in 2026 (where YMPE = $74,600), the statutory ceiling 2.5 × YMPE equals $186,500. Under ITR subsection 2900(8), if the specified employee is employed by associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, this single 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500) ceiling must be shared across the entire associated corporate group.

Government Assistance, the Grind Rule, and ITC Recapture
Government Assistance and Subsection 127(18) Reduction Mechanics

To prevent the stacking of public subsidies beyond statutory limits, the Income Tax Act enforces a comprehensive coordination regime governing government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments. Under subsection 127(9), "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—including funding distributed by a non-profit organization that receives its underlying funds from a government organization.

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the ITA, both the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure base for ITC purposes must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance (defined with reference to inducements or reimbursements under paragraph 12(1)(x)), or contract payment that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of the corporate income tax return for the year. When the amount of assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceeds the SR&ED expenditures of that project, subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's length party to nil. Where assistance applies across a non-arm's length corporate group, members may allocate the reduction using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Conversely, when a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED pool, the repayment increases the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and restores qualified expenditure eligibility in the year of repayment.
Strategic Stacking with NRC IRAP and Government Loans

A cornerstone of Canadian innovation finance is stacking federal SR&ED tax credits with direct non-repayable grants from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which reimburses up to 80% of internal technical salaries and up to 50% of subcontractor costs. Under the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, while an IRAP grant reduces total qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18), if the claimant elects the Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated on the full, unreduced eligible SR&ED salary base prior to deducting the IRAP grant. For example, if a CCPC incurs $100,000 in direct SR&ED salaries and receives an $80,000 IRAP salary grant, the unreduced SR&ED salary base of $100,000 still generates a 55% PPA of $55,000, bringing gross qualified expenditures to $155,000. Subtracting the $80,000 IRAP assistance under subsection 127(18) leaves $75,000 in net qualified expenditures, earning $75,000 × 35% = $26,250 in refundable SR&ED ITCs on top of the $80,000 IRAP grant.

Corporate claimants must also exercise diligence when accepting government loans or conditionally repayable contributions. Under the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and Tax Court jurisprudence, conditionally repayable contributions—and government loans featuring patient or concessionary repayment terms—are generally treated as government assistance that reduces the subsection 37(1) pool and subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures in the year received, with the SR&ED expenditure base only replenished in future years as repayments are made (though recent statutory amendments for specific concessionary loans allow claimants who deducted such loans on Form T661 to amend returns for years that are not statute-barred).
The Provincial-Federal Grind Rule and Subsequent-Year Taxability

Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits meet the statutory definition of "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), provincial R&D tax credits and federal SR&ED ITCs are not simply additive. Under subsection 127(18), the provincial R&D tax credit earned on a given dollar of expenditure reduces ("grinds") the federal qualified expenditure base for that same taxation year, unless the taxpayer formally renounces the provincial R&D tax credit on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return. Mathematically, if a corporation earns a provincial R&D tax credit at rate rprov and a federal SR&ED ITC at rate rfed on an identical expenditure base, the combined effective credit rate rcombined is governed by the Grind Formula:
rcombined = rprov + rfed × (1 − rprov)

To illustrate, for a British Columbia CCPC incurring $1,000,000 in qualified SR&ED expenditures within the $6 million expenditure limit, the corporation earns a 10% B.C. SR&ED tax credit of $100,000. Under subsection 127(18), that $100,000 provincial credit reduces the federal qualified expenditure base from $1,000,000 to $900,000, resulting in a 35% federal SR&ED ITC of $900,000 × 35% = $315,000 and a combined federal and provincial refundable benefit of $100,000 + $315,000 = $415,000 (an effective combined rate of 41.5%).

Furthermore, federal SR&ED ITCs claimed to reduce tax or refunded in cash in Year 1 trigger a mandatory tax adjustment in the following taxation year (Year 2). Under paragraph 37(1)(c) of the ITA, the federal ITC claimed or refunded in Year 1 reduces the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in Year 2. To the extent that the subsection 37(1) pool was already fully deducted in Year 1—which occurs automatically for the portion of the ITC earned on the non-pooled Prescribed Proxy Amount—the resulting negative pool balance is included directly in the corporation's taxable income in Year 2 pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA (or reduces the UCC of depreciable capital or shared-use equipment property).
Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(35))

When a claimant earns an SR&ED ITC on a physical asset or transformed material and subsequently sells that property or converts it to commercial use within 20 taxation years of earning the credit, subsection 127(27) of the ITA triggers ITC Recapture. Rather than merely reducing the section 37 deduction pool, recaptured ITCs under subsections 127(27), 127(29), or 127(34) are added directly to the taxpayer's Part I federal tax otherwise payable on Line 602 of the T2 corporate income tax return.

Under the CRA Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, the categories of property subject to subsection 127(27) recapture encompass materials for SR&ED that are transformed and included in a custom product, commercial asset, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development; all-or-substantially-all (ASA) capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024; shared-use equipment (SUE); animals and other growing things used in SR&ED projects; and physical property acquired through a contract involving SR&ED. Crucially, however, the CRA policy confirms that where intellectual property (IP) belongs to the payer under the terms of an R&D contract, the payer is not "acquiring" the IP because the IP always belonged to the payer and simply accrues as it is generated; consequently, there is zero ITC recapture when the payer disposes of the IP or converts it to commercial use.

For standard ASA property or materials transformed, the recaptured amount under subsection 127(27) is the lesser of the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the particular property, and the applicable SR&ED ITC rate (such as 35% or 15%) multiplied by either the proceeds of disposition (if disposed of to an arm's-length person) or the fair market value of the property at the time of conversion or transfer (if converted to commercial use or sold to a non-arm's length party). For instance, if a claimant earned a 35% ITC on $300,000 of expenditures ($105,000 ITC) that included $135,000 of materials transformed into an experimental unit, and subsequently sold or converted those transformed materials at full value, the recapture is 35% of $135,000, or $47,250. For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), paragraph 127(27)(d) and subsection 127(33) stipulate that recapture occurs only when the SUE is sold to an arm's-length person or when all or substantially all of the property is converted to commercial use (such that SR&ED usage becomes merely incidental), and only the qualified percentage of the proceeds of disposition or fair market value (25% if claimed only for the first term, or 50% if claimed for both the first and second terms) is included in the recapture calculation. Thus, if a corporation earned $28,000 of ITCs across both terms on SUE and later sold the property at arm's length for $100,000, the recaptured ITC is the lesser of $28,000 and 35% × $100,000 × 50% = $17,500. Companion provisions govern recapture where qualified expenditures were transferred between non-arm's length parties under subsection 127(29) and subsection 127(34), or incurred through partnerships under subsection 127(30).
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (2025–2026 Landscape)

Every Canadian province except Prince Edward Island (along with the Yukon Territory) supplements the federal SR&ED program with its own R&D fiscal incentive. While most provinces harmonize directly with the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and administer their credits jointly through the CRA via T2 corporate schedules, Quebec (administered independently by Revenu Québec via the CO-17 return) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance via the AT1 return) operate autonomous provincial filing regimes.
Quebec's 2025–2026 Structural Overhaul: The CRIC Regime

In the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget, the Quebec Ministère des Finances announced a sweeping restructuring of provincial innovation incentives, replacing its fragmented network of legacy R&D tax credits with a single, unified incentive: the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, or CRIC). The CRIC applies to taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025.
Abolition of Seven Legacy Quebec Tax Measures

To simplify compliance and redirect fiscal support toward higher-value-added commercialization, the introduction of the CRIC simultaneously abolished seven legacy Quebec innovation tax measures for taxation years starting after March 25, 2025: the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R-D) (Form RD-1029.7); the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6); the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03); the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1); the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credits (retaining only the fashion design component); and the personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and foreign experts.
Expanded Scope: R&D, Pre-Commercialization, and Capital Expenditures

Unlike the federal SR&ED program—which terminates where experimental development concludes and pre-production or commercialization begins—Quebec's CRIC bridges the commercialization gap by covering three distinct pillars of activity carried out in Quebec by corporations (excluding tax-exempt entities, Crown corporations, and corporations controlled by prescribed research entities). First, the CRIC covers scientific research and experimental development (R&D) salaries, a portion of payments to Quebec subcontractors, and payments to eligible research entities. Second, the CRIC covers eligible pre-commercialization activities (activités de précommercialisation)—work carried out in continuity of R&D such as product testing, technological validation, regulatory homologation, certification, and prototyping to bring an innovation to market. Third, the CRIC renders eligible certain capital expenditures tied to the acquisition of depreciable property used in Quebec R&D and pre-commercialization activities, aligning with the federal restoration of capital expenditures.
Modified Exclusion Threshold, Rates, and Revenu Québec Forms

To focus tax assistance on higher-value-added jobs, the CRIC applies a modified exclusion threshold (seuil d'exclusion) to each taxation year or fiscal period equal to the greater of $50,000 (prorated for the number of days in a short taxation year) or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold (calculated from the basic personal tax credit amount applicable to the involved employees). Once a qualified corporation's net eligible expenditures exceed this exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit at an enhanced rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of net eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold (allocated among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN), and a base refundable rate of 20% on all excess eligible expenditures above $1,000,000. If a corporation claims the CRIC as a member of a qualified partnership, the enhanced 30% rate does not apply and the flat 20% refundable rate governs its share of partnership expenditures. Corporations claim the CRIC with their Quebec CO-17 corporate return by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR (English courtesy translation RD-1029.8.CR-T, Codes 112 and 113), accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.PR (RD-1029.8.PR-T) for pre-commercialization activities and Form RD-222 for the deduction of Quebec R&D expenditures.
Ontario: Dual-Credit Architecture (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits through the CRA via schedules attached to the T2 corporate return. Crucially, Ontario has not adopted the federal $6 million expenditure limit, retaining its independent statutory caps and phase-out corridors. The first program is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566), which provides an 8% refundable tax credit for CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure cap of $3,000,000 (yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000). The $3 million OITC expenditure limit phases out when the associated corporate group's prior-year Ontario taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

The second program is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508), which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit to all corporations (CCPCs and non-CCPCs alike) with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, with no upper expenditure limit. Because the OITC is government assistance, a CCPC claiming both credits must deduct its 8% OITC from its qualified expenditure base before computing the 3.5% ORDTC on Schedule 508 (though neither the OITC, ORDTC, nor OBRITC reduces the OITC base itself). Unused ORDTC credits carry back 3 years and carry forward 20 years against Ontario corporate income tax. The third program is the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedule 568 (accompanied by Schedule 569 for each eligible contract), which provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible R&D contract with an approved Ontario post-secondary or hospital research institute.
British Columbia: Budget 2026 Permanent Alignment (Bill 2)

Governed by Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and amended by Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit was made permanent in B.C. Budget 2026 and fully aligned with the federal Bill C-15 reforms for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in British Columbia may claim a 10% refundable tax credit on the lesser of their B.C. qualified SR&ED expenditures and the federal expenditure limit—which increased to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—phasing out over the expanded prior-year taxable capital corridor of $15 million to $75 million. Expenditures in excess of the $6 million limit, as well as eligible B.C. expenditures incurred by non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations, earn a 10% non-refundable B.C. tax credit. Bill 2 also restored the eligibility of capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, as B.C. qualified expenditures. Corporations claim the B.C. credit by filing Form T666 and entering the non-refundable credit on Line 659 and the refundable credit on Line 674 of T2 Schedule 5 no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29)

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Alberta claim provincial R&D support separately from the federal T2 return by filing Alberta Form AT1 Schedule 29 (alongside AT1 Schedule 13) with the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return. The Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable grant delivered through the corporate tax system equal to 8% on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (calculated as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two preceding taxation years), plus an enhanced 20% refundable rate on incremental Alberta R&D spending exceeding that two-year average, up to an annual expenditure cap of $4,000,000. The IEG phases out for corporations whose taxable capital lies between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000.

body.text: CRA Administration, Form T661 (Version 26), and the April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process
The Statutory 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Form T661 (26)

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after its taxation year-end, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline falls strictly 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures were incurred. To access SR&ED tax incentives, a corporate claimant must submit both Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations)—or Form T2038(IND) for unincorporated individuals—on or before this 18-month reporting deadline.

On May 15 and May 25, 2026, the CRA released an updated Form T661 (Version 26), alongside updated versions of Schedule T2SCH31, Form T1145, Form T1146, the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, and the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, accompanied by interim line-by-line filing instructions while Guide T4088 undergoes revision. Version 26 of Form T661 adds dedicated lines for the Pre-Claim Approval Case Number, the field of research code, capital expenditures, shared-use equipment, and post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs. In Part 2 (Project Data) of Form T661, claimants must substantiate each project within strict word limits: up to 350 words describing the technological advancements sought (Line 240/246), up to 350 words articulating the technological obstacles or uncertainties that had to be overcome (Line 242), and up to 700 words summarizing the systematic investigation and experimental work performed in the taxation year to overcome those uncertainties (Line 244).
The Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Announced in the 2025 Federal Budget (Canada Strong) and officially launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the Pre-Claim Approval Process provides businesses with upfront technical certainty by evaluating whether planned R&D projects meet SR&ED eligibility requirements before work begins or significant costs are incurred.
Eligibility Criteria for Pre-Claim Approval

To qualify for optional pre-claim approval, the applicant business must be a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership; must have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000; and must be in good compliance standing with the CRA. Furthermore, the submitted project (up to a maximum of three projects per application) must be planned or only recently initiated, must not have been included in any previous SR&ED claim, and must not involve issues currently under litigation.
Four-Step Workflow, Service Standards, and 90-Day Fast-Track Processing

The pre-claim approval pathway operates through a four-step workflow. First, the claimant completes a brief online eligibility web form (taking less than five minutes) to request a case number, which the CRA issues within two to five business days. Second, the claimant completes and uploads the application for up to three projects using existing internal project documentation via the CRA My Business Account portal. Third, within four weeks of submitting the application, a CRA SR&ED Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) contacts the claimant to schedule a direct technical consultation meeting—which is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and discretionary for existing claimants in good standing. Fourth, within eight weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the CRA issues a written pre-claim approval determination.

If granted, pre-claim approval remains valid for up to three taxation years (if denied, there is no formal Notice of Objection process at the pre-claim stage, though the taxpayer may still submit a standard post-year-end SR&ED claim). While a business granted pre-claim approval must still submit Form T661 after year-end to claim its incurred expenditures, any claim containing pre-approved projects that is selected for an expenditure review has its CRA processing service standard cut in half from 180 calendar days down to 90 calendar days. Concurrently with the April 1, 2026 pre-claim launch, the CRA expanded its deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) risk screening to route low-risk claims to "accepted as filed" processing within 60 calendar days, updated The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (replacing The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants), and maintained its free First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) for newly filing innovators.
Landmark Jurisprudence and Tax Court of Canada Audit Precedents

Because subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED in broad conceptual terms, the operational boundaries of technological uncertainty, systematic investigation, and contemporaneous documentation have been forged by the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC)—relying on Information Circular 86-4R3 and unanimously affirmed as binding national law by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393—Justice Donald Bowman established the five-question judicial test that governs every CRA technical review and Tax Court appeal. First, was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Third, did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, rather than ad hoc trial and error? Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement—recognizing explicitly that the conclusive rejection of a hypothesis constitutes a valid technological advancement because it eliminates unviable pathways and advances general technological understanding? Fifth, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?
Evolution of Software, Shop-Floor, and Evidentiary Jurisprudence (2006–2025)

Subsequent decisions of the Tax Court of Canada have refined the application of Northwest Hydraulic across software engineering, industrial shop-floor manufacturing, food science, and evidentiary procedure. In Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597 (2007 DTC 41), the Tax Court addressed software development claims, holding that the satisfactory use or integration of existing software tools to build a commercial program does not establish technological uncertainty unless underlying system constraints cannot be resolved through publicly available knowledge, while also illustrating the litigation hazard of a taxpayer failing to object to a CRA employee testifying as an expert witness. Similarly, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (affirmed 2011 FCA 355), both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed a claim involving shop-floor modifications to manufacturing machinery where iterative mechanical adjustments were performed without formulating and testing explicit scientific hypotheses.

In contrast, in Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, Justice Gaston Jorré delivered a landmark ruling in favour of a Montreal electric motor and appliance subassembly manufacturer (49% owned by General Electric), allowing all disputed shop-floor SR&ED claims and awarding litigation and expert witness costs against the Crown. Abeilles established five critical legal principles for corporate claimants: projects must be assessed holistically as a whole and across multiple taxation years rather than "de-constructed" into isolated sub-steps until no eligibility remains; the need to develop a commercially viable, cost-effective, high-productivity, and flexible manufacturing process can constitute a valid factor of technological uncertainty; a diligent search by the taxpayer demonstrating a lack of solutions in the public domain is adequate evidence of technological uncertainty; while contemporaneous documents are needed to corroborate SR&ED, they do not require special SR&ED-specific formatting provided they cross-link the claimed work to the timeframe of the claims; and CRA employees lack the institutional independence required to serve as neutral expert witnesses in Tax Court.

In the years following Abeilles, the Tax Court continued to police the boundary between routine engineering and documented experimentation. In Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65 (2015 DTC 1089), the Court dismissed a software claim where the appellant lacked contemporaneous records substantiating systematic hypothesis testing. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, the Court held that custom-engineering bespoke theatrical rigging systems using standard engineering principles constituted routine engineering rather than SR&ED. In Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32, the Court reiterated that technological uncertainty must be objective rather than a mere lack of internal familiarity within the claimant company.

In Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 (2023 DTC 1069), Chief Justice Eugene Rossiter overturned the CRA's denial of seven experimental food-manufacturing projects conducted between 2013 and 2016 (totalling $343,449 in disallowed expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs excluding 2014) involving the formulation of custom frozen pies for major retailers including Costco and Loblaws. Chief Justice Rossiter noted at paragraph 89 that while the lacking knowledge must exist in the objective base of scientific or technological knowledge, Canafric systematically analysed why specific ingredient formulations failed and adjusted parameters accordingly. Crucially, the Court held that failed recipes that allowed Canafric to eliminate unviable formulations constituted a valid technological advancement, and ruled that detailed, factually grounded oral testimony by the company's CEO (Mr. Pandya) paired with contemporaneous formulation test records satisfied the fifth criterion. Most recently, in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63, the Tax Court denied an oilfield frac water heater claim due to a lack of documented experimentation, while in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173, the Court upheld reassessments clawing back approximately $738,000 in previously paid SR&ED refunds 7 to 10 years after the original taxation years, underscoring the enduring audit exposure of unsubstantiated claims.

body.text: Strategic Audit Synthesis and Compliance Recommendations

The convergence of the Bill C-15 legislative reforms (enacted March 26, 2026), the CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (launched April 1, 2026), the May 2026 Form T661 (Version 26) rollout, British Columbia's Bill 2 alignment, and Quebec's CRIC regime necessitates a coordinated compliance strategy for Canadian corporate taxpayers. First, hardware, manufacturing, clean-tech, and life-sciences corporations must audit all capital asset acquisitions and equipment leases entered into after December 15, 2024, implementing contemporaneous utilization logs to substantiate either the ≥ 90% All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) threshold or the > 50% to < 90% Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) threshold across the first and second 12-month periods. Second, scaling CCPCs whose balance-sheet taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000—alongside newly eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs) with average gross revenues below $75,000,000—should model the three-year average gross revenue phase-out election to preserve access to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and up to $2,100,000 in annual 35% refundable federal credits.

Third, private corporations employing shareholder-researchers (specified employees) must structure founder remuneration through regular T4 base salary paid within 180 days of fiscal year-end rather than dividends or bonuses, ensuring that Form T1174 and certified directors' resolutions are filed before the 18-month reporting deadline whenever a specified employee works across associated corporations. Fourth, eligible corporations and partnerships with gross business income under $25,000,000 initiating novel R&D projects should leverage the optional Pre-Claim Approval pathway in My Business Account to lock in an eight-week upfront technical determination valid for up to three years and halve any subsequent financial review timeline from 180 days to 90 days. Finally, software and industrial claimants alike must enforce strict cloud-resource tagging (development/SR&ED versus production/COGS) and maintain contemporaneous records of failed hypotheses and experimental test logs in their natural project management environments to satisfy the evidentiary standards reinforced in Abeilles, Canafric, and Vortex Energy Services.
